 Canada’s 2026 budget sets aside $142 billion for tax changes including May 15 deadline
 Analysis 
 6 November 2026 
 i 
 Prime Minister Mark Carney and Minister of Finance and National Revenue Francois-Philippe Champagne in Ottawa, Nov. 4, 2025. Justin Tang/The Canadian Press.
 Prime Minister Mark Carney and Minister of Finance and National Revenue Francois-Philippe Champagne in Ottawa, Nov. 4, 2025. Justin Tang/The Canadian Press.
 The Hub Staff 
 View bio 
 06 Nov 26 
 Article 
 Summary 
 Key Stats 
 The Carney government’s 2026 federal budget, tabled Thursday, would give every individual taxpayer a single May 15 deadline to file and pay, starting with returns for the 2027 tax year due in spring 2028. It also announces plans to merge registered retirement savings plans (RRSPs) and registered retirement income funds (RRIFs) into an “RRSP for life,” so retirees would no longer have to convert their accounts at 71.
 The changes are part of what the 511-page budget, titled “Masters of Our Destiny,” bills as the most ambitious tax-simplification effort in decades. Overall, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne’s plan contains $142.1 billion in new tax incentives, spending and other measures over five years, plus $9.4 billion announced since the spring economic update.
 The package adjusts filing rules, retirement accounts and business incentives rather than redesigning the tax code. Charles Lammam , who has argued in a series of Hub essays this year for structural tax reform, wrote after the budget that Ottawa spent nearly all of an unexpected fiscal windfall rather than using it to shrink deficits.
 One deadline for everyone 
 Under current rules, most individuals must file and pay by April 30. Self-employed people and their spouses or common-law partners have until June 15 to file but must still pay any balance by April 30 or face arrears interest, currently 7 percent and compounded daily.
 Under the proposal, all individuals, including the self-employed, would file and pay by May 15. The budget says giving filers and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) more time to receive and process tax slips will reduce reassessments and interactions with the agency. The government estimates the change will help Canadians avoid $230 million in interest and penalties over five years.
 The budget also raises instalment thresholds for individuals and corporations and gives most taxpayers one year after a notice of assessment to file an objection.
 RRSP for life 
 The retirement change is less settled. The budget announces the government’s intention to merge the tax rules for RRSPs and RRIFs, which would eliminate the need to convert at 71. It would also let a surviving spouse or partner become the successor holder of an RRSP and simplify tax-free transfers to survivors.
 It would not let retirees shelter savings indefinitely. The Globe and Mail reports minimum withdrawal requirements would remain, and no draft legislation or start date has been published. RBC Wealth Management describes the merger as headed for consultation.
 The budget also enriches the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit, the GST/HST credit the government renamed in January , including a one-time payment in early 2027, and offers children free museum access.
 Business incentives draw mixed reviews 
 The business centrepiece is a new Canada Growth Incentive. Its banner measure exempts up to $15 million in capital gains on eligible investments. Qualifying shares must be issued by a Canadian-controlled private corporation between budget day and the end of 2036, the company’s assets cannot exceed $100 million when they are issued, and investors must hold them for at least 36 months.
 Ottawa expects the exemption to cost $80 million in 2029-30 and $485 million in 2030-31. The budget also makes the existing small-business capital gains rollover more flexible.
 Jean-François Ruel, senior economist at the Canadian Tax Observatory, told The Canadian Press the exemption “reduces the cost of investing” by cutting investors’ tax on exit. Randall Bartlett, deputy chief economist at Desjardins Group, told the wire service the measures should lift business investment, but modestly.
 Dan Kelly, president and chief executive of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, didn’t find much to help SMEs. “While there’s a mega deduction and there’s a focus on mega projects, my takeaway is that this is a mega disappointing budget for small business owners,” he told The Canadian Press . The federation’s own statement nonetheless said the $15-million exemption could spur small-business investment if properly designed.
 Windfall spent, reform deferred 
 Lammam’s post-budget analysis found Ottawa now expects $158 billion more over five years than it did in the spring and puts $152 billion of it, or 96 cents of every extra dollar, into new spending and tax measures. Five-year deficits end up only about $7 billion smaller, while public debt charges climb to $85.5 billion by 2030-31.
 He had laid out the case for bigger changes before the budget. In a January DeepDive , he argued that U.S. tariffs and American tax changes were drawing capital south. “We are in a war for capital, and we are losing,” he wrote.
 In June , he pointed to a decade of layered changes: a capital gains inclusion rate hike announced and later reversed, bare trust reporting rules introduced then suspended, new cross-border rules and an overhauled Alternative Minimum Tax. The result, he argued, is a system so complex that “the government doesn’t always know how to administer it.”
 Service data support that concern. Complaints to the taxpayers’ ombudsperson rose 27 percent in 2025-26, the highest level in three years, with processing delays the largest driver.
 The auditor general’s October 2025 audit of CRA contact centres found the agency fielded more than 32 million calls in 2024-25 and answered just over 10 million. When auditors tested agents with general individual-tax questions, they answered correctly 17 percent of the time.
 That came as the CRA’s workforce grew roughly 31 percent in a decade, from about 40,000 employees in 2015 to 52,500 in 2025 . The government launched a 100-day service improvement plan in September 2025, which Lammam acknowledged has produced modest gains such as longer chat hours and a callback pilot.
 Whether a later deadline eases tax season may depend on whether the agency keeps pace. The single deadline would first apply to returns filed in spring 2028. The RRSP merger has no legislation or start date.

 Canada’s 2026 federal budget, presented by Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, allocates $142.1 billion for tax changes and incentives over five years, introducing a unified May 15 deadline for all taxpayers. Key reforms include merging RRSPs and RRIFs into an ‘RRSP for life’ and enhancing business incentives, although some critics argue the budget falls short for small businesses. The government anticipates that these changes will simplify tax processes and reduce penalties for Canadians. However, concerns remain about the complexity of the tax system and the effectiveness of the Canada Revenue Agency’s service improvements.
 $230 million in interest and penalties are expected to be avoided over five years due to the new filing deadline.
 Complaints to the taxpayers’ ombudsperson rose 27 percent in 2025-26, the highest level in three years.
